12425-de-orbe-novo-volume-1-of-2-the-eig:
Francis Augustus MacNutt's 1912 translation brings Peter Martyr d'Anghera's De Orbe Novo, the Eight Decades, into English from Latin, with notes and introduction. Martyr, born at Arona in 1457 near Lago Maggiore, wrote letters and decades on the new world as news reached Spain.

Volume one opens with bibliography and the first three decades, illustrated by portraits such as Cardinal Ascanio Sforza and Leo X. Martyr's pages report voyages, peoples and courts in the voice of a well-placed observer. MacNutt's edition makes a key early source on discovery readable for English students, with scholarly help at hand.
12725-the-vale-of-cedars-or-the-martyr:
Grace Aguilar's 1851 Vale of Cedars, or The Martyr, opens with a memoir of its author. Aguilar was born at Hackney on 2 June 1816, eldest child and only daughter of Emanuel Aguilar. Her father descended from Spanish Jews who fled persecution and found asylum in England. She lived with delicate health from infancy, spending summers by the sea on physicians' advice.

The novel that follows, set among Spanish Jews, tells of faith, love and martyrdom. A Byron verse serves as epigraph: the wild dove has her nest, the fox his cave, mankind their country, Israel but the grave. Aguilar writes with earnest, domestic piety. The book remains a classic of Anglo-Jewish historical fiction, tender toward a persecuted people.
26129-john-hus-a-brief-story-of-the-life:
William Dallmann's short life of John Hus, published at St. Louis in 1915, tells how a peasant boy from Husinec in Bohemia rose through the University of Prague to become a preacher who challenged the church of his day. Hus took in the writings of Wyclif, offended the clergy, faced charges laid before the pope, and was at last excommunicated and driven into exile.

The later chapters follow him to the Council of Constance, where he was tried in chains, refused to take back his views, and was condemned and burned on July 6, 1415. Written in plain chapters for general readers, the book keeps its focus on Hus's steady courage and on why later reformers counted him a martyr.
31236-martyr:
Alan E. Nourse's story, printed in Fantastic Universe in January 1957, opens four and a half hours after Martian sunset, as the last light in the Headquarters Building blinks out. Carl Golden stamps his feet against the cold, watching a girl leave and start down the frosty road toward the colony lights. After she goes, he waits ten minutes more, then crosses to peer through a lobby window at a call-board of colored studs.

The magazine's blurb frames the larger fight. Rejuvenation is for the millions, or for five hundred lucky ones treated each year, with Senator Dan Fowler battling alone against a clique seeking perpetual power and perpetual youth. Hard-hitting and conspiratorial, the tale turns a Mars colony into a stage for political thriller.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beda-mayr:
Beda Mayr was a Bavarian Benedictine philosopher, apologist, and poet, born near Augsburg in 1742, who died in 1794. He took vows at Heiligenkreuz in 1762, was ordained in 1766, and taught mathematics, philosophy, rhetoric, theology, and canon law there. An exemplary religious and popular preacher, he absorbed Kant's subjectivistic criticism as a philosopher and was irenic beyond measure as a theologian.

In a letter to Henry Braun, he argued that Catholic-Protestant unification was possible, and Braun published it without consent in 1778. Augsburg's bishop censured him and temporarily barred him from teaching theology. His chief work, defending natural, Christian, and Catholic religion in three parts (1787-90), was placed on the Index in 1792. Lindner counts fifty-eight productions, including twenty-one dramas and four sermon volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confession-bu:
F. M. Rudge's entry traces confession, from Latin confessio, first a martyr's burial place, also called memoria or martyrion. Use widened over time to the altar over the grave, the underground chamber holding the tomb, and the high altar over the confession. Later it meant the basilica itself, and finally a new resting place after transfer. On transfer, relics went to a crypt below the high altar, or a hollow beneath it, behind a pierced screen, as in the catacombs.

The tomb stayed open, touched by the faithful with brandea cloths, later venerated as relics. At Saint Clemente the urn of Clement and Ignatius shows behind such a screen. Confession lamp oil counted as relic. Rome's famed underground confessions include San Martino ai Monti, San Lorenzo with Laurence and Stephen, and Santa Prassede with Praxedes. Greatest stands Saint Peter's, where Anacletus raised a memoria and Constantine built the Confession.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-neumayr:
Franz Neumayr, born at Munich on 17 January 1697 and died at Augsburg on 1 May 1765, was a Jesuit preacher, writer, and dramatist of sacred plays in Latin. He entered the Society on 3 October 1712 and taught rhetoric and belles-lettres for ten years. He preached on missions for two, then directed Munich's celebrated Latin sodality with high credit for eleven years. From 1752 to 1763 he preached at Augsburg Cathedral with extraordinary success. His controversial sermons against Lutheran teachings, above all against the apostate monk Rothfischer and Chladonius, baffled adversaries by solidity of argument.

His output astonishes: Latin plays for his sodality, staged for Munich's literary men, sermons from Augsburg pulpit, ascetical works, treatises on rhetoric and poetry. Essays on moral theology defending the Jesuit system complete the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-thur:
Johannes Thurmayr, called Aventinus from his birthplace Abensberg, was Bavaria's first great historian. Born in 1477, he studied at Ingolstadt, Vienna, Cracow, and Paris, tutored the younger brothers of Duke William IV, and in 1517 became historiographer of Bavaria, charged with writing the country's history. Many sources he collected survive only in his copies.

His Annales Bojorum carried Bavarian history to 1460 with a critical use of sources, and his condensed German version, the Bavarian Chronicle, was the first important history written in German. Though he ranked as a Catholic, he sympathized with the humanists and reformers, rejected auricular confession, and attacked pilgrimages, indulgences, and what he called excessive claims of the hierarchy. His history therefore appeared only in 1554, with hostile passages cut, and the Chronicle in 1566.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martyr:
Martyr comes from Greek martus, a witness testifying from personal observation. In early Christian writing the apostles were witnesses of all they saw in Christ's public life and learned from his teaching, in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and to earth's uttermost part. 

Only by degrees in the Church's first age did martyr come to mean solely those who died for the faith, and the orthodox were not allowed to seek martyrdom. In antiquity, accepting state religion bound every citizen, and refusing the gods counted as treason. Later edicts hardened: Severus barred becoming Christian, Decius in 250 opened a deadlier regime of special edicts, Valerian struck in 257, and Diocletian's last persecution from 284 to 305 proved severest. Of 249 years from Nero in 64 to Constantine's peace in 313, Christians suffered repeated persecution, yet no firm total of martyrs exists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-edmund-the:
Edmund, king of East Anglia, died at twenty-nine rather than buy peace on terms his faith forbade. Crowned about 855 at only fifteen, he ruled justly, shut his ears to flatterers, and spent a year at Hunstanton learning the whole Psalter by heart for daily prayer. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 gives his death at Hoxne on 20 November 870.

In that year the Danish chiefs Hinguar and Hubba invaded, were repulsed, then returned in overwhelming force. To spare a fruitless massacre, Edmund disbanded his troops and withdrew toward Framlingham. Captured on the way, he refused their terms and was killed. Later legend made him a Saxon prince born at Nuremberg, but the earliest accounts root him among East Anglia's own kings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-edward-the:
Edward the Martyr, king of England for only three and a half years, was murdered at eighteen in a succession plot. Son of Edgar the Peaceful, he was crowned by Dunstan after his father's death in 975. A party led by his stepmother Elfrida opposed him, wanting her own seven-year-old son Ethelred crowned instead. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 gives his death as 18 March 979.

Though barely thirteen at his accession, Edward won his people's affection by virtue and promise. Hunting in Dorset, he called at Corfe Castle, where Elfrida lived. Drinking mead on horseback at the gate, he was stabbed by an assassin. He rode off, fell from his horse, and died. The entry is brief, but it fixes a murder that stained a queen and made a boy king a saint.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-justin-mar:
Justin Martyr, second-century apologist, tried Stoic, Peripatetic, Pythagorean, and Platonist teachers before finding Christianity. Born at Flavia Neapolis about 100, converted about 130, he taught and defended the faith in Asia Minor and at Rome, dying a martyr about 165. Two Apologies and his Dialogue with the Jew Tryphon survive. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his feast to 14 April, set by Leo XIII with a Mass and Office.

In his own writings Justin gives personal details of philosophy studies and conversion, though partly idealized, not straight life story, and poetry must be separated from truth. A Stoic taught him nothing about God. A Peripatetic demanded a fee, proving no philosopher. A Pythagorean required music, astronomy, and geometry first. A Platonist delighted him for a time. The account, the entry says, arranges facts to show pagan philosophy's weakness beside prophets and Christ. His martyrdom documents are undisputed.
the-vale-of-cedars-or-the-martyr:
Grace Aguilar's The Vale of Cedars, or The Martyr, appeared in 1851 with a memoir of the author placed before the story. Aguilar was born at Hackney on June 2, 1816, eldest child of Emanuel Aguilar. Her family descended from Jews of Spain who fled persecution and found asylum in England.

The memoir stresses a contrast between frail health and an early, eager mind. Sickly from infancy, she spent summers by the sea under doctors' care, yet learned to read almost without trouble and asked always for books as presents. Her mother was nearly her only teacher. She kept a journal from age seven and, before twelve, had begun writing, already observant on family tours of English cathedrals and manufactories.
